Hi Mina,

Thanks again for the product demo this week — the team was impressed with the routing/fallback behavior and the KV cache profiling. Before we proceed to the procurement side, our infra and procurement teams need clarity on the latency SLOs you can commit to for the hosted API (we are shipping a patient-facing triage flow at scale). Specifically:

- Can you confirm p50 and p95 targets we can rely on for text generation (single-turn, ~256 tokens)?
- How do you measure those numbers — rolling windows, aggregation rules, and how are regional differences handled?
- Are there standard carveouts for transient cold starts, burst traffic, or datastore backpressure?

We are trying to map these commitments to our internal SLAs. If you can provide a short proposal (including any temporary exceptions for initial onboarding) that would help speed approval.

Hi Sofia — really appreciate the clear ask and the context about the triage flow. I chatted with Karthik and Ben and we put together a short proposal below; attaching a draft SLA and a workbook with example measurement windows.

High level proposal (hosted API, single-turn, 256-token gen):
- Contractual commitments (reported monthly): p50 <= 60ms, p95 <= 420ms (US regional endpoint).
- Operational SLO (rolling telemetry for alerting): p50 <= 55ms, p95 <= 350ms (rolling 60-minute windows for detection).
- Measurement method: 28-day reporting window for billing/contract purposes (median-of-daily p50/p95 aggregation), with a 60-minute rolling window used for alerts and immediate remediation triggers.
- Regional handling: commitments are per-region. If Catalyst routes to us via US-east only, the above applies. Cross-region deployments can have separate commitments per region.
- Carveouts & exceptions: agreed temporary carveouts for provider-side cold starts, infra upgrades, and cloud provider maintenance windows. We propose a 90-day onboarding grace window where we allow up to 1% of p95 violations per week to be excluded while we warm caches and tune batching.

Fallbacks & mitigation: automatic routing to a low-latency model variant for 99.5% of degraded incidents; prefix caching for repeated queries; throttling controls exposed to your engineers.

Next steps we recommend:
1) Review attached SLA draft (redwood-sla-draft-v1.pdf).
2) Look at the measurement workbook (measurement-windowing-workbook.xlsx) to validate the aggregation rules against your traces.
3) If the 90-day onboarding grace looks acceptable, we can bake it into the contract as a Temporary Performance Carveout (TPC).

Attaching the two files. Happy to hop on a short call this week to walk through the workbook.

Best,

Thanks Mina — this is helpful. A few clarifying questions from our infra team after looking at the workbook:

- The difference between the "operational SLO" (rolling 60m) and the "contractual commitment" (28-day reporting) is sensible, but we need to understand how the aggregation works. Example: if on one day we have sustained 10-minute bursts where p95 spikes to ~900ms due to a cache warm-up, how does that affect the monthly reported p95?

- For the 90-day onboarding grace: is the proposed "up to 1% of p95 violations per week" applied to the 60m rolling windows or to daily aggregates? We also need to know whether that carveout is automatically applied or requires an exception request after an incident.

- Can you confirm whether cold-starts from new model variants (e.g., switching quantization profiles or fallback routing) are included in the measurement or considered separate transient events?

We're trying to avoid surprises in the contract language — if you can show a short worked example in the workbook (one row per day, calculation of monthly p95 with our burst scenario) that would be ideal.

Also looping in our procurement ops mailbox for visibility.

Best,

Sofia

Hi Sofia — looping in a short, concrete example and a recommended measurement rule set from our SRE playbook.

Worked example (simplified):
Day 1: p95 = 380ms (normal)
Day 2: short 10-min burst, p95 (day) = 900ms
Day 3–28: p95 daily values between 340–410ms

Monthly reported p95 calculation (proposed): compute daily p95 per region, then report the 28-day median of those daily p95 values. In the scenario above the single-day 900ms spike produces one daily value of 900ms; the 28-day median would therefore remain near the normal range provided the rest of the days are within target. This approach prevents single transient bursts from driving the contractual metric while preserving sensitivity to sustained degradation.

On the 90-day onboarding carveout: the "1% of p95 violations per week" we proposed is applied to the weekly count of 60-minute rolling windows that exceed the operational p95 threshold. If you see internal telemetry showing significant sustained deviations beyond the 1% allowance, we expect a joint post-mortem and an official exception request to be raised (we can automate the exception detection and draft submission). The carveout is not automatic forever — it is a time-limited allowance to reduce friction during ramp.

Cold-starts from new model variants: modeled cold-starts (new weights / quantization changes) are considered transient events and marked with a specific event tag in our telemetry; we exclude those tagged events from contractual aggregation provided they are flagged and reviewed within a 7-day window. That requires a short pro forma operational change: a Canary & Flagging run during deploys that your team can sign off on.

Recommended contractual language snippet (for the SLA):
"For the first 90 days following initial production traffic ramp, Redwood and Customer agree to a Temporary Performance Carveout (TPC) allowing up to 1% of 60-minute rolling telemetry windows to be excluded from contractual p95 calculations, provided that such events are disclosed and reviewed in the agreed post-mortem process."

If that sounds good, Mina and I can prepare an annotated SLA for signature and a short runbook for your infra team describing the event tagging process.

Thanks,
